references.text: The psalmist asks rhetorically whether the one who formed the ear should not hear, and the one who shaped the eye should not see. This affirms God's sovereignty over human senses, just as in Exodus 4:11.
David describes how God formed him in his mother's womb and knit him together. This demonstrates God's creative power over the human body and its abilities.
Proverbs declares that the Lord has made both the ear that hears and the eye that sees, a direct parallel to God's statement that He gives humans mouth, sight, and hearing.
Isaiah receives a message to make the people's ears dull and their eyes blind. This shows God's power over human ability to hear and see.
The prophecy that the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped shows that God, who created these abilities, can also restore them.
The Lord's servant will open blind eyes. This confirms God's authority over sight and blindness.
God refers to a people who have eyes but do not see, and ears but do not hear. God has power over both physical and spiritual sight and hearing.
The disciples ask who sinned so that the man was born blind. Jesus answers that it happened so that God's works might be displayed, demonstrating God's sovereignty over blindness.
Paul uses the image of a potter shaping clay to illustrate God's sovereign right to shape people as He wills, including their abilities and limitations.
Confirms the same theological principle of God's absolute sovereignty over human speech and voice.
Jesus' healing of the blind man is a concrete fulfillment of God's sovereign power over sight as described in Exodus.
Connects God's sovereign creation of human conditions with His special attention to the brokenhearted.
Concrete examples of God's power to open a mute mouth, confirming the claim made in Exodus.
